content: Monitoring progress in the provision of health services in prisons and other closed settings is essential. As previously mentioned, it is critical to collect data on the availability and quality of services in these environments. Disaggregating data by setting—such as prisons versus community settings—can help identify disparities in access to healthcare and assess whether the principle of equivalence of care is being upheld. Additionally, disaggregating data by geographic area, such as rural versus urban regions, is important for many countries to guide decisions on where services should be located. This is particularly relevant due to the differing characteristics and needs of populations in these areas. Setting targets for key indicators is a strategic approach to planning an effective response to the HIV epidemic. Targets can be established for intervention indicators, such as availability, coverage, and quality of services, as well as for enabling environmental factors like legislative changes. Outcome and impact indicators, such as reductions in new HIV infections or changes in risk behaviors (e.g., consistent condom use), are also critical. These targets help identify areas requiring attention and guide programmatic responses to meet high-level commitments, such as those outlined in the United Nations 2011 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS. The 2011 Political Declaration set ambitious goals to be achieved by 2015, including reducing sexual transmission of HIV by 50%, halving HIV transmission among people who inject drugs, eliminating new HIV infections among children, and reducing maternal deaths. Other goals included providing antiretroviral treatment to 15 million people living with HIV, halving tuberculosis deaths among people with HIV, closing the global AIDS resource gap, eliminating gender inequalities and violence, and addressing HIV-related stigma and discrimination. UNAIDS launched the Fast-Track Targets in 2014 to mobilize global efforts to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030. These targets include ensuring that by 2020, 90% of people living with HIV know their status, 90% of those diagnosed receive treatment, and 90% of those on treatment achieve viral suppression. By 2030, these targets increase to 95% for each category. Additional goals include reducing new HIV infections among adults in lowand middle-income countries to 500,000 per year by 2020 and 200,000 per year by 2030, and achieving zero discrimination by repealing discriminatory laws and policies. Target-setting must reflect local factors, such as the nature of the HIV epidemic, the current stage of the response, available resources, and structural factors influencing risk and intervention impact. Countries should undertake a collaborative process involving community-led organizations, government representatives, and other stakeholders to set realistic yet aspirational targets. This process includes assessing the current scale of the response, evaluating available resources, and determining the potential for scaling up interventions. Strengthening systems for program monitoring may also be necessary to track progress toward these targets. Indicators for assessing the enabling environment, service availability, and quality are essential for measuring the impact of efforts to address HIV among key populations, including men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Auditing current legislation and policies is crucial to identify laws that may negatively impact key populations or hinder HIV prevention efforts. For example, laws criminalizing consensual same-sex acts, sex work, or drug use can create barriers to accessing services. Conversely, supportive legislation, such as laws protecting against discrimination or ensuring access to healthcare for people in prisons, can enhance the response to HIV. Countries should aim to introduce supportive policies and remove harmful ones, setting realistic timeframes for reform and monitoring progress. These services may include pro bono legal aid, community paralegals, and access to traditional dispute resolution mechanisms. Support services for individuals from key populations who experience violence should include medical, psychological, and legal assistance. Sensitization training for law enforcement officers on the rights and needs of key populations is also critical. Programs providing services to key populations should adhere to quality standards, including anti-discrimination policies, meaningful involvement of key population representatives, and mechanisms for anonymous client feedback. Services should be accessible without restrictions based on age, gender identity, sexual orientation, or other factors, and should be provided at no cost or at an affordable rate. In summary, setting and monitoring targets for HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care requires a comprehensive approach that considers the unique needs of key populations and local contexts. Collaborative efforts, supportive legislation, and high-quality, accessible services are essential to achieving global and national goals to end the AIDS epidemic.
